analysis.one_liner: Requires credit card companies to warn customers before raising rates and to disclose terms in ads.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: after one subcommittee hearing in October 1991, it sat in the House Banking Committee until the Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required credit card companies to tell customers, in their monthly statements, before any change to their account terms — including interest rate increases — took effect. Cardholders who received a rate-increase notice could keep their old rate on the existing balance by closing the account. It also would have required key terms to be printed in a standard table on application envelopes and spoken or shown in credit card radio and TV ads.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card holders. In 1991 issuers could raise a card's interest rate at any time and apply it to balances already racked up, with no advance notice. This bill would have forced 30 days' notice and let customers lock in their old rate on the existing balance by stopping use of the card [S2][S3]. Simpler, standardized disclosure on envelopes and in ads would also make comparison shopping easier [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Before a card issuer could change any account term, including the interest rate, the change would have to appear in the cardholder's monthly statement in a standard table — so the change could not take effect silently [S2][S3].

A cardholder notified of a rate increase could elect to stop using the card, and the outstanding balance would stay at the old rate instead of jumping to the new one; using the card again would end that protection and trigger liability for the forgone interest [S2][S3].
Rate increases and other adverse changes could not take effect until 30 days after the cardholder received notice, giving customers time to pay down or move a balance [S3].

Credit card applications and solicitations would have to carry key terms in a standard table on the envelope, and radio and TV credit card ads would have to disclose rates and fees, making offers comparable at a glance or a listen [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers — banks and other lenders that profit from raising rates on existing balances — would lose the ability to reprice debt without notice, and customers who elected the old rate would pay less interest. Issuers would also bear the cost of new statement, envelope, and advertising disclosures, which they could pass along to customers in other fees [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill requires new tabular disclosures on every statement, application envelope, and broadcast ad, which imposes ongoing compliance costs on issuers and production costs on broadcasters; those costs can be passed to consumers through other fees [S3].

The rescission right protects only customers who stop using the card entirely — any new purchase voids the old-rate protection and makes the customer liable for the difference in interest — so the safeguard is most useful to people who can pay off or move their balance, not those who must keep borrowing [S2][S3].

By restricting issuers' ability to reprice existing balances, the bill could lead lenders to charge higher rates upfront or tighten who gets credit at all, a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real but modest: notice before rate hikes and a one-time chance to keep the old rate on an existing balance. The disclosure mandates are cheap per customer and address a genuine problem — in 1991, terms could change silently. The main limitation is that the rescission right is all-or-nothing and helps most those who can stop using the card. On balance, the benefits to cardholders outweigh the compliance costs, though it stops well short of capping rates or fees.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking Committee and its consumer affairs subcommittee, which held one hearing in October 1991, and nothing further happened before the two-year Congress ended — no markup, no floor vote, no Senate action.

narrative.text: Rep. Chuck Schumer (D-NY) introduced the bill on May 22, 1991, and it was referred to the House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs [S1][S5].
Sixteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill [S4].
On June 3, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Affairs and Coinage, which held hearings on October 9, 1991 [S5].

No further action was recorded — the committee never voted to report the bill, the House never debated it, and the Senate never considered it before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers came out ahead: without the bill, they kept the ability to raise interest rates on existing balances with no advance notice and no way for customers to lock in the old rate. Cardholders who would have gained from the notice and rescission rights got nothing.

for.name: Subcommittee on Consumer Affairs and Coinage
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on October 9, 1991.

against.name: House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill in May 1991, held no markup, and never reported it to the House floor.

against.name: Credit card issuers and banks
against.what_they_did: Had a strong financial stake in blocking the bill, since it would end unannounced rate increases on existing balances; the record does not show their lobbying, but the bill died without ever reaching a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 cosponsors were House Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; with no recorded votes, the bill never drew a formal partisan test [S4].

industries.industry: Credit card issuers (banks and consumer lenders)
industries.note: Issuers in 1991 could raise a card's interest rate at any time and apply the new rate to balances customers had already built up. The bill would have required 30 days' notice and let customers keep the old rate on their existing balance by closing the account — directly cutting into revenue from rate hikes.

The bill would have required credit card ads to include verbal or on-screen disclosure of rates and fees, adding production and compliance burden to broadcast advertising. The cost is small and the broadcasters' interest does not run against consumers, but it is a real cost to the industry.
